Chapter 4. The Moral Crisis: Conscience Versus Custom.
Sooner or later, we all reach a moment where what’s right crashes head-on with what we’ve always done. For so many people, the rules of caste feel like they’re part of nature itself—almost as if they’re moral truths. But every now and then, something cuts through the haze. You see someone suffering, and suddenly, tradition isn’t a good enough excuse anymore.
Picture this: there’s a teacher, someone respected in his town. At first, he just accepts how things are. But he starts noticing the little cruelties—some kids are always made to sit at the back, their voices go unheard, and worst of all, they’re made to feel less, just because of who they are.
He tries to shrug it off, telling himself, “Well, that’s just the way it is.” But then he sees the pain in those kids’ eyes, and suddenly, the old explanations don’t cut it. He starts to wonder—can tradition ever make cruelty okay?
Here’s something to pay attention to: most of us don’t realize how easy it is to just go along with unfairness, simply because it’s what we’re used to. The fear of being the odd one out, or being called a troublemaker, keeps a lot of folks quiet. But have you noticed how conscience always finds a way to speak up—even in the stillness of the night?
That teacher? He can’t sleep anymore. He’s haunted by the feeling that, without even meaning to, he’s become part of a system that hurts innocent people.
Some say the caste system is needed for order—that it keeps society running smoothly. But think about the cost: millions of people living without dignity, just so the system can keep rolling along. The real question isn’t whether the system works. It’s whether the system is just.
What becomes clear is this: true morality can’t lean only on what’s always been done. Every tradition needs to answer one simple test—does it respect the dignity and rights of every single person? If keeping a custom means we have to silence our conscience, then maybe it’s the custom that needs to change.
This tug-of-war between conscience and custom isn’t just something we wrestle with alone. It’s a challenge for all of us. It takes real courage to speak out, to stand up for people who are pushed down, and to demand a world where everyone is treated as an equal. It means realizing that the old rules don’t get to decide our future.
